title: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the equatorial plane.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the fact is that the chromatin substance now _behaves_ after the fashion of a “diamagnetic” body, and is repelled from the stronger to the weaker parts of the field.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Nucleus and chromatin in the field”. Scope: nuclei and chromosomes of dividing cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern mitosis datasets can strongly test whether known mechanical machinery explains equatorial movement and thereby refute the claimed necessity. Direct confirmation of a diamagnetic mechanism would require physical measurements not usually present.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track chromosomes during mitosis and compare their trajectories with quantitative predictions of repulsion from a bipolar field versus motor- and microtubule-based transport. Perturbing spindle microtubules or motors should leave field-driven equatorial collection intact but disrupt a mechanical mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Diamagnetic' is an analogy without a calibrated field variable.

Most images do not measure electromagnetic susceptibility.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public mitosis movies can confirm the kinematic half, collection toward the equator, for many cell types. They cannot show that chromatin is diamagnetic, and the rival mechanical account predicts the same positions. The claim is therefore only partly resolvable: the path is testable, the physical kind of force is not, without new susceptibility measurements.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track chromatin position through prometaphase and test whether chromosomes move from the poles toward the equatorial plane as a diamagnetic body would, using magnetic susceptibility if the analogy is taken literally. Equatorial collection that disappears when microtubule attachment is removed, with no diamagnetic susceptibility of the required sign, would refute the physical reading; motion that follows an applied magnetic gradient as predicted would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The wording is explicitly an analogy, 'after the fashion of' a diamagnetic body.

Equatorial congress is also the prediction of microtubule attachment and congression.

Magnetic susceptibility of chromatin during mitosis is not an archived variable.
